Prelims: the founders of Vijayanagara, the Bahmani capitals, and the battle of Talikota. Mains: discuss the role of Vijayanagara in the political and cultural life of the south.
How to answer

“Vijayanagara administration: nayankara system.” “Why did Vijayanagara fall at Talikota?” “Mahmud Gawan’s reforms.” Prelims tip: Harihara-Bukka 1336; Bahmani 1347; Gawan; Krishnadevaraya 1509 to 29; Talikota 1565; Amuktamalyada; Paes and Nuniz.
Delhi Sultanate Administration
How the Sultans ruled

The Sultanate (1206 to 1526) built institutions that Akbar later inherited. UPSC asks about iqta, the army, revenue reforms of Alauddin, central departments and the role of ulema and nobles. Know the Sultan-wise reforms.
The Sultan and the nobles

The Sultan was supreme head, claiming authority from the Caliph (Iltutmish was confirmed by the Abbasid caliph, 1229). Nobility: Turks, later Khaljis, Afghans and Indian Muslims. Balban developed the theory of kingship with sijda and paibos ; Chihalgani (the Forty) were Iltutmish’s nobles, broken by Balban.
Central departments

Wazir (finance; Diwan-i-Wizarat), Ariz-i-mamalik (army; Diwan-i-Arz), Diwan-i-Risalat (religious matters and appeals), Diwan-i-Insha (correspondence). Sadr-us-sudur headed charity. Barid-i-mumalik headed spies. Alauddin set up Diwan-i-Mustakhraj (arrears); Firoz added Diwan-i-Khairat and Diwan-i-Bandagan.
Iqta system

Introduced by Iltutmish : a muqti received revenue of an area (iqta) in place of salary, collected taxes, kept troops and sent surplus. Transfer every few years. Balban checked muqtis; Alauddin reduced their powers; Firoz Tughluq made iqta hereditary; Sikandar Lodi tightened accounts.
Central officers
Alauddin Khalji’s reforms

Standing army paid in cash (dagh, horse branding; chehra, soldier rolls); price control (market controls for grain, cloth, horses, slaves) under the Shahna-i-mandi ; revenue measured land ( masahat ), one-half of produce as kharaj ; tax on houses ( ghari ) and grazing ( chari ). Intermediaries (khuts, muqaddams) were curbed.
Muhammad bin Tughluq and Firoz

Muhammad bin Tughluq tried token coinage, moved the capital to Daulatabad (1327), raised the Doab tax; faced rebellions, and he introduced agricultural loans ( taqavi ). Firoz Tughluq built canals (Hisar), 300 towns, imposed jizya on Brahmins too, abolished some cesses and set up employment bureaus.
Theocracy or secular?

Writers like Ziauddin Barani wanted an Islamic state. Modern historians (Mohammad Habib, K. A. Nizami, Irfan Habib) note a pragmatic state that relied on zawabit (secular regulations) over sharia. Jizya was collected, but rulers rarely demanded religious conversion.
Legacy

Land revenue measurement, mansabdari ancestors (dagh), Persian as court language, the rupee (tanka and silver coin by Sher Shah) and the postal system (dak chowki) all descend from the Sultanate. Modern terms like “Diwan” and “Pargana” remain.
Iqta and the Sultan’s power

The Sultans ruled through the iqta system. An iqta was an assignment of land revenue to an officer, called an iqtadar or muqti. The officer collected the revenue, kept a share to pay his troops and sent the rest to the treasury. A worked example. Suppose an iqta yields 100 units of revenue. The muqti keeps 60 units to pay his troops and sends 40 to the treasury. The treasury gets 40 out of 100, which is 40 per cent of the revenue. A sharp distinction: iqta and jagir. An iqta was a revenue assignment that the Sultan could move. Under the Mughals, jagirs did a similar job. The idea was alike, but the rules and records differed. A famous case: Alauddin’s army. Alauddin kept a large standing army and paid it in cash. This reduced the officers’ ability to build their own armies on the basis of their iqtas. Exam trap. An iqta was not a permanent estate passed down a family. It was a revenue right that the state could take back. How it is asked. Prelims: the iqta system and the Sultanate dynasties. Mains: examine the administrative system of the Delhi Sultanate.
How to answer
“Examine Alauddin Khalji’s market reforms.” “Assess the iqta system.” Prelims: dagh, chehra, jizya, Barani, Ariz-i-mamalik. Mains: Nature of the Sultanate state.
Vijayanagara Art and Architecture
Hampi and a style

Vijayanagara (1336 to 1565) created a distinctive style at Hampi and in Andhra and Tamil Nadu. Questions ask about Hampi monuments, temple features, Krishnadevaraya’s patronage, gopurams and musical pillars . Hampi is a World Heritage Site (1986).
Hampi, the royal centre

Hampi on the Tungabhadra (Karnataka) has two parts: the sacred centre (Virupaksha, Vitthala, Hemakuta) and the royal centre (Lotus Mahal, elephant stables, Mahanavami Dibba, Queen’s bath). Foreign travellers Domingo Paes and Abdur Razzak praised its size and wealth.
Key temples

Virupaksha (Pampapati, Shiva), Vitthala temple (c. 16th century, stone chariot, musical pillars), Hazara Rama temple (a thousand Ramayana panels), Krishna temple built by Krishnadevaraya in 1515, Achyutaraya temple, giant monolithic Narasimha and Ganesha. Veerabhadra at Lepakshi (Andhra).
Architectural features

Blended Dravida with Deccani Islamic style. Features: tall raya gopurams (Krishnadevaraya’s gateways at Kalahasti, Kanchi, Chidambaram, Tiruvannamalai), kalyana mandapas (marriage halls with composite pillars), amman shrines for goddess, pillared corridors , horse-rearing pillars with rearing yalis, and Indo-Islamic arches in secular buildings like the Lotus Mahal.
Hampi complexes
Sculpture and painting

Large bas-reliefs and dwarapalas, yali pillars, Bhakti-themed bronzes (Krishnadevaraya and his queens, Tirumala). Lepakshi murals in the Veerabhadra temple are major Vijayanagara paintings. Dance and music were patronised, and Telugu literature flourished (Krishnadevaraya’s Amuktamalyada, the Ashtadiggajas).
Water and fortification

Hampi’s canals, stepped tanks and aqueducts were fed from the Tungabhadra by anicuts (Turtha canal). Fortification walls and gates enclosed the city in seven lines (Paes). Defeat at Talikota (1565) led to its sack, leaving the present ruins.
Indo-Islamic influence

George Michell and others note Deccani influence in secular buildings, while temples stay Dravidian. Some argue Vijayanagara’s architecture is pure “Hindu empire”; others see it as a composite culture. “Sewell’s A Forgotten Empire” (1900) popularised the site.
Today

Hampi (Group of Monuments at Hampi, UNESCO 1986) draws tourists; the Hampi Utsav and the Vijayanagara empire’s 650th-year events recall it. ASI and the Hampi World Heritage Area Management Authority protect it. Lepakshi (Andhra) is on the tentative list; the Basavanna bull is a major attraction.
The stone chariot at Hampi

Vijayanagara architecture is known for large temples and pillared halls. The Vittala temple at Hampi, with its stone chariot, is the best-known example. A worked case: the stone chariot. The chariot is a stone shrine carved to look like a wooden car, with stone wheels. The temple’s musical pillars give out different notes when they are struck. Both show the skill of the stone-carvers. A sharp distinction: the mandapa. Vijayanagara temples often have a mandapa, a pillared hall, in front of the shrine. Some halls were used for music, dance and rituals. The style mixed features from earlier southern traditions. Lepakshi. The Veerabhadra temple at Lepakshi in Andhra Pradesh has a hanging pillar, which does not touch the floor, and a large mural painting. Exam trap. Hampi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed in 1986. It was built by Vijayanagara rulers, not the Delhi Sultanate. Do not mix them. Why it matters. The Hampi style shows how kings used art to show power, wealth and devotion at the same time. How it is asked. Prelims: Hampi, the Vittala temple, Lepakshi and UNESCO listings. Mains: discuss the features of Vijayanagara art and architecture.
How to answer
“Vijayanagara temple architecture and Dravida synthesis.” Prelims: Vitthala temple, Hazara Rama, Lotus Mahal, Lepakshi. Mains: Evaluate Krishnadevaraya as patron of art and literature.
The Mughal Empire: Polity and Administration
The great early modern empire
The Mughals ruled most of India for about 180 years at their peak. Administration (mansabdari, revenue) and culture are tested every year.
Establishment

Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) , Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527), Afghans at Ghaghra (1529). Humayun lost to Sher Shah at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540), returned in 1555. Sher Shah Suri (1540 to 45): Grand Trunk Road, rupiya , dam , a revenue system based on measurement, and sarais . Humayun’s regaining of Delhi in 1555.
Akbar (1556 to 1605)

Second Battle of Panipat (1556) with Bairam Khan. Conquests: Malwa, Gondwana, Chittor (1568), Gujarat, Bengal, Kashmir, Kandahar, Khandesh. Religious policy: abolished the pilgrim tax (1563) and jizya (1564); Ibadat Khana (1575); mahzar (1579); Din-i-Ilahi (1582); sulh-i-kul (peace with all). Court: Abul Fazl, Faizi, Todar Mal, Birbal, Tansen, Man Singh. Rajput alliance.
Mansabdari system

Mansab = rank. Two numbers: zat (personal rank and pay) and sawar (cavalry to be kept). Ranks from 10 to 10,000 (princes higher). Paid by jagirs (revenue assignments) or cash; dagh and chehra continued. Transferable and non-hereditary. Under Shah Jahan, the month scale ( masik ) and sihbandi . The jagirdari crisis under Aurangzeb (shortage of jagirs) is linked by Satish Chandra to the decline.
Land revenue and economy

Todar Mal ’s zabt (Akbar’s Dahsala , 1580): measured land, average prices and yields of ten years, revenue in cash (about one-third of produce). Other systems: batai , kankut , nasaq . Crops: wheat, rice, cotton, indigo, sugarcane; new: tobacco, maize, chillies. Trade with Europeans brought silver. Cities: Agra, Lahore, Surat. Craft: cotton textiles of Bengal and Gujarat. The zamindars were intermediaries.
Central and provincial administration

Emperor ( Padshah ), Wakil , Diwan-i-Kul (finance), Mir Bakhshi (army), Sadr-us-Sudur (religious grants), Mir Saman (household), Qazi-ul-Quzat (justice). 12 subas by Akbar, later more; Subadar , Diwan , Bakhshi , Faujdar , Kotwal . Sarkars and parganas; Amil and qanungo . A centralised system with checks.
Later Mughals

Jahangir (1605 to 27): chain of justice, Nur Jahan’s role, painting; Sir Thomas Roe’s embassy (1615). Shah Jahan (1628 to 58): Taj Mahal, new city Shahjahanabad; war of succession (1657 to 58). Aurangzeb (1658 to 1707): reimposed jizya (1679), temple controversies, Deccan campaigns (Bijapur 1686, Golconda 1687), revolts of Jats, Satnamis, Sikhs (Guru Tegh Bahadur’s execution 1675), Marathas, Rajputs; the Deccan ulcer.
Why did the Mughal Empire decline?

Irfan Habib ( Agrarian System of Mughal India ) stresses an agrarian crisis from heavy revenue demands. Satish Chandra points to the jagirdari crisis. M. Athar Ali emphasises the growth of the nobility. Others (Jadunath Sarkar) blamed Aurangzeb’s religious policy; modern scholars (Muzaffar Alam, C. A. Bayly, Chetan Singh) point to regional powers rising and the shift of power to provinces. Balanced answers use several causes.
Why it matters today

The Mughal revenue records ( Ain-i-Akbari ), the idea of an empire-wide administration and the language Urdu (Hindustani) are living legacies. The Grand Trunk Road survives as NH 1 and NH 2. Debates about historical figures in textbooks and place names make the Mughals a political subject. The Red Fort is the site of Independence Day.
Mansabdari: rank, troops and pay

The mansabdari system gave every Mughal officer a rank. The rank set pay, status and the number of troops the officer had to keep. Akbar built this system in the 1570s. A worked case: zat and sawar. A mansabdar’s zat was his personal rank. His sawar was the number of horsemen he had to maintain. For example, a man with 1,000 zat and 500 sawar had to keep 500 horsemen. A sharp distinction. Zat decided status and a large part of salary. Sawar decided the military duty. Higher sawar ranks were paid more, but the exact rules changed over time. Land revenue. Akbar’s minister Todar Mal introduced the zabt system and the dahsala method, around 1580. The dahsala method fixed rates from the average of ten years of prices and yields. Exam trap. Zabt and dahsala are often mixed up. Zabt is the system of measuring and assessing. Dahsala is the ten-year average used for the rates. Why it matters. The rank tied an officer’s pay to the state. This kept the army under central control. How it is asked. Prelims: mansabdari, zat, sawar, and dahsala. Mains: discuss the mansabdari system and its role in the Mughal state.
How to answer

“Mansabdari system: features and problems.” “Was Akbar’s religious policy a political strategy?” “Causes of the decline of the Mughal Empire.” Prelims tip: Panipat 1526, 1556; Chausa 1539; Khanwa 1527; Haldighati 1576; Dahsala 1580; zat and sawar; Ain-i-Akbari (Abul Fazl).
Marathas and the Decline of the Mughals
The challengers
The Marathas, Sikhs and regional nawabs filled the space left by the Mughals. They matter to the story of how the British found it easy to expand.
Rise of Shivaji

Shivaji (1630 to 1680), son of Shahaji Bhonsle, took Torna (1646) and built Raigad. Killed Afzal Khan (1659). Attacked Surat (1664); Treaty of Purandar (1665) with Jai Singh; visited Aurangzeb at Agra (1666) and escaped. Coronation at Raigad (1674) as Chhatrapati. Southern campaign (Jinji, Vellore, 1677 to 78).
Shivaji’s administration

Ashtapradhan : Peshwa (prime minister), Amatya, Mantri, Sachiv, Sumant, Senapati, Pandit Rao, Nyayadhish. Revenue: ryotwari -like, with chauth (one-fourth) and sardeshmukhi (extra one-tenth) from neighbouring territory. Salaried army, strong forts, navy (Kanhoji Angre later). Reduced the role of deshmukhs and abolished jagirs. Hill forts and guerrilla war ( ganimi kava ).
After Shivaji

Sambhaji executed in 1689; Rajaram; Tarabai. Shahu was released in 1707; civil war with Tarabai; Treaty of Warna (1731) split Kolhapur and Satara. Peshwas from Balaji Vishwanath (1713 to 20) took control: Baji Rao I (1720 to 40), Balaji Baji Rao (1740 to 61). Maratha confederacy: Scindia (Gwalior), Holkar (Indore), Bhonsle (Nagpur), Gaekwad (Baroda). Raids reached Delhi, Orissa, the south.
Panipat 1761 and after

At the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated the Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau and Vishwasrao. About 100,000 died. It broke Maratha reach and weakened the north. Mahadji Scindia revived their power; Nana Phadnavis in Pune. Three Anglo-Maratha wars: 1775 to 82 (Treaty of Salbai), 1803 to 05, 1817 to 18, ending Maratha power.
Mughal decline and successor states

After Aurangzeb (1707) came weak rulers. Nadir Shah sacked Delhi (1739; took the Peacock Throne). Abdali’s raids. Successor states: Bengal (Murshid Quli Khan), Awadh (Saadat Khan), Hyderabad (Nizam-ul-Mulk, 1724), Rohillas, Jats (Suraj Mal), Sikhs (Ranjit Singh later), Mysore (Haidar Ali), Travancore (Marthanda Varma). The Mughal emperor became a figurehead; Shah Alam II.
Sikhs and Jats

Guru Nanak, Guru Arjan (Adi Granth, 1604; killed 1606), Guru Hargobind, Guru Tegh Bahadur, Guru Gobind Singh (Khalsa, 1699; died 1708). Banda Bahadur’s rebellion (1709 to 1716). Misls in the 18th century; Ranjit Singh (1799 to 1839) unified the Punjab, the Sikh Empire. The Jats (Gokula, Raja Ram, Churaman, Suraj Mal at Bharatpur).
Who is to blame for decline?

Jadunath Sarkar blamed Aurangzeb; Marxist writers (Irfan Habib) blamed the jagirdari and agrarian crisis. Revisionists (Chetan Singh, Muzaffar Alam, C. A. Bayly) see an 18th-century of regional growth and new prosperity, not a dark age. On the Marathas, Grant Duff praised Shivaji; Govind Sakharam Sardesai and Jadunath Sarkar both studied them. Was Shivaji a Hindu or a national king? Historians (Satish Chandra) say a regional ruler with secular practice, including Muslims in the army.
Why it matters today

Shivaji is a regional and national icon; Maharashtra’s politics uses his memory (statue and memorial debates). The Khalsa and Gurdwara reform shape Sikh identity; Ranjit Singh’s legacy is a Punjab emblem. Federal power-sharing between the centre and regional power has roots in this age. Indian Navy’s new ensign (2022) draws on Shivaji’s seal.
Chauth and sardeshmukhi

Shivaji built a Maratha state in the 1660s and 1670s. He did so partly by taxing other lands. The two main claims were chauth and sardeshmukhi. A worked case: chauth. Chauth was one-fourth of the land revenue. The Marathas took it from areas outside their control, in return for a promise not to raid. For example, if the revenue was 400 units, the chauth was 100 units. A sharp distinction. Sardeshmukhi was an extra 10 per cent, claimed as a hereditary right of the sardeshmukh. Shivaji claimed this right over the Deccan. Together, the two claims made the Marathas a major power. A famous battle: Panipat, 1761. An Afghan army led by Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated the Marathas, led by Sadashivrao Bhau. The loss hit Maratha leadership hard and let other powers grow. Exam trap. The Maratha Confederacy was a group of chiefs under the Peshwa, not one state with one ruler. Do not say that Shivaji ruled a confederacy. How it is asked. Prelims: chauth vs sardeshmukhi, and the battle of Panipat (1761). Mains: examine the reasons for the rise of the Marathas and the decline of the Mughal empire.
How to answer

“Assess Shivaji’s administration.” “Why did the Marathas fail to build an all-India empire?” “Eighteenth century India: dark age or transition?” Prelims tip: Panipat 1761; Ashtapradhan; chauth and sardeshmukhi; Nadir Shah 1739; Khalsa 1699; Hyderabad 1724; Treaty of Purandar 1665.
Mughal Architecture
A tested evolution
Mughal architecture is a staple of Prelims. The question is usually who built what, material, and features . Track the path from red sandstone (Akbar) to white marble (Shah Jahan).
Babur and Humayun

Babur built mosques at Panipat (Kabuli Bagh) and Sambhal and gardens (charbagh). Humayun’s Tomb , Delhi (1565–72, built by Haji Begum, Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas): first garden-tomb, red sandstone with white marble; double dome; UNESCO site 1993. Sher Shah built the Qila-i-Kuhna and his tomb at Sasaram, an octagonal tomb on a lake.
Akbar

Red sandstone, fusion with Hindu and Gujarati styles. Agra Fort ; Fatehpur Sikri (1571–85): Buland Darwaza (1576, victory over Gujarat), Jama Masjid, Diwan-i-Khas, Panch Mahal, Jodha Bai’s palace, Salim Chishti’s tomb in white marble; Akbar’s tomb at Sikandra (Agra). Fatehpur Sikri was abandoned due to water shortage.
Jahangir and Nur Jahan

Itimad-ud-Daulah’s tomb (Agra, 1622–28, by Nur Jahan): first Mughal building entirely in white marble with pietra dura inlay (parchin kari); sometimes called the “baby Taj”. Gardens: Shalimar Bagh and Nishat Bagh, Kashmir. Jahangir’s tomb at Lahore.
Evolution
Shah Jahan

The golden age of Mughal architecture: Taj Mahal (1632–53, Ustad Ahmad Lahori; double dome, minarets, four-part charbagh; UNESCO 1983), Red Fort and Jama Masjid in Delhi, Moti Masjid in Agra, Diwan-i-Aam and Khas (“If there is a paradise on earth…”), Shalimar Bagh Lahore, Peacock Throne. The city Shahjahanabad (1648).
Aurangzeb and decline

Badshahi Mosque (Lahore, 1673), Moti Masjid in the Red Fort, and Bibi ka Maqbara (Aurangabad), a weak copy of the Taj built by his son Azam Shah. Royal patronage declined, but regional Mughal styles flowered in Awadh (Bara Imambara, Lucknow) and the Deccan.
Persian or Indian?

Features are Persian (charbagh, iwan, double dome, pietra dura) but craftsmen and motifs are Indian (chhatris, jharokhas, brackets, lotus). Percy Brown called it a synthesis. Gardens symbolised paradise; the Taj plan shows the river-side garden, unlike the usual tomb at the centre.
Today

The Taj Mahal, Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri, Humayun’s Tomb and Red Fort are UNESCO sites. Taj Trapezium Zone rules limit pollution near the Taj (M. C. Mehta case, 1996). The Red Fort hosts the Independence Day speech; it was taken up under the “Adopt a Heritage” scheme (2017).
Why the Taj stands out

Mughal architecture grew over about 150 years. It began with the tombs of Babur’s and Humayun’s time. Each ruler left buildings that showed his style and power. A worked case: Humayun’s tomb. It was built in Delhi in the 1560s by Humayun’s widow, Haji Begum. It has a charbagh garden, split by water channels into four parts. Its design served as a model for later tombs, including the Taj Mahal. A sharp distinction: the Taj Mahal. Shah Jahan built it from about 1632 to 1653 as a tomb for Mumtaz Mahal. It is white marble with inlay. The dome, the minarets and the charbagh garden are its key features. Exam trap. The Taj is a tomb, not a palace or fort. The Red Fort in Delhi is a different building, a palace-fort built by Shah Jahan. A famous debate. Mughal architecture is often called Indo-Islamic. Some scholars stress Persian roots, others stress the work of Indian craftsmen and motifs. Both views are debated. How it is asked. Prelims: Humayun’s tomb, the Taj Mahal and their builders. Mains: discuss the evolution of Mughal architecture and the blend of Persian and Indian features.
How to answer
“Trace evolution of Mughal architecture.” Prelims: first garden tomb (Humayun’s), first marble (Itimad), Buland Darwaza. Mains: Mughal synthesis in architecture, with examples.
Maratha Administration
Shivaji’s state-building

Shivaji (crowned 1674) built a compact, centralised, tax-based state. UPSC asks about the Ashta Pradhan, chauth and sardeshmukhi, forts, navy and the Peshwa period . It also appears with the Maratha Military Landscapes World Heritage listing.
Rise and coronation

Shivaji, born 1630 at Shivneri to Shahaji and Jijabai, took Torna (1646), killed Afzal Khan (1659), fought Shaista Khan (1663), signed the Treaty of Purandar (1665) and escaped from Agra (1666). He was crowned at Raigad on 6 June 1674 by Gaga Bhatt as Chhatrapati , and died in 1680.
Ashta Pradhan

A council of eight ministers, with no hereditary posts: Peshwa (prime minister), Amatya (finance), Mantri (the king’s records), Sachiv (correspondence), Sumant (foreign affairs), Senapati (commander-in-chief), Pandit Rao (religion, charity), Nyayadhish (justice). Ministers were advisers, not independent. Many held military commands.
Revenue

Based on Malik Ambar’s ryotwari-type system with measurement by rod ( kathi ); cultivators paid directly to officials, not jagirdars. Shivaji abolished the role of hereditary deshmukhs. Chauth (one-fourth of revenue) and Sardeshmukhi (an additional 10 per cent) were levied on neighbouring non-Maratha areas, and in return protection was offered.
Ashta Pradhan
Army, forts and navy

Cavalry were paga (regular, paid by the state) and silahdar (irregular, own horses). Infantry were the mavli . Forts: Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Sindhudurg, with three officers sharing power (havaldar, sabnis, karkhanis). The navy at Kolaba and Sindhudurg under Kanhoji Angre later. Guerrilla war ( ganimi kava ).
Peshwa and confederacy

After Shahu (1707 to 1749), power passed to the Peshwas of Pune: Balaji Vishwanath (Treaty of 1719), Baji Rao I (1720 to 40), Balaji Baji Rao (Nanasaheb), who lost the Third Battle of Panipat (1761). A confederacy of Scindia (Gwalior), Holkar (Indore), Gaekwad (Baroda), Bhonsle (Nagpur) grew. The Anglo-Maratha Wars (1775–1818) ended it.
Hindu swaraj or a revenue state?

Nationalist historians such as G. S. Sardesai and Ranade praised Shivaji as a national hero. Marxists note a revenue-extracting state with peasant misery. Jadunath Sarkar was critical but also admiring. Debate also exists on whether he was a Hindu-nationalist or inclusive (he employed Muslims in his army and navy).
Today

In July 2025 UNESCO inscribed the Maratha Military Landscapes of India (12 forts, including Raigad, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Sindhudurg and Gingee) as a World Heritage Site. Shivaji’s coronation anniversary is a Maharashtra festival. The Indian Navy’s emblem was redesigned in 2022 inspired by Shivaji’s seal.
The eight ministers and the forts

Shivaji’s government had a council of eight ministers, called the Ashta Pradhan. Each minister had a set duty, such as finance, the army or foreign affairs. The council advised the king. It did not rule on its own. A worked case: the forts. Shivaji built or took many forts. Raigad became his capital. Sindhudurg, built on an island off the Konkan coast in the 1660s, shows his interest in naval power. A sharp distinction: Ashta Pradhan and Peshwa. Under the later Peshwas, power moved to one minister, the Peshwa. The other ministers lost influence. The state became more of a confederacy of chiefs. Revenue. Shivaji’s officers measured the land and fixed a share of the crop to be paid. Rules varied from area to area. Exam trap. The Ashta Pradhan was an advisory body. Do not say that its members ruled the country. Why it matters. Shivaji’s council shows a ruler who took advice from many experts but kept the final decision himself. How it is asked. Prelims: the eight ministers and their roles, and forts such as Raigad and Sindhudurg. Mains: discuss Shivaji’s administrative system, its strengths and its limits.
How to answer
“Examine Shivaji’s administration.” Prelims: Ashta Pradhan names, Chauth, Treaty of Purandar, Raigad. Mains: How far was the Maratha state different from the Mughal?
The Sikh Gurus
Faith, politics and a state

The ten Gurus built a distinct faith, scripture and later a political power. Prelims asks about each Guru’s contribution and Mughal confrontations. It links with Bhakti and the Punjab freedom struggle.
Guru Nanak (1469–1539)

Born at Talwandi (Nankana Sahib). Taught Ik Onkar , equality, naam japna, kirat karna, vand chakna . Founded Kartarpur (on the Ravi), started langar . Rejected caste, idols, asceticism. Four udasis (journeys). Succeeded by Angad.
Gurus 2 to 4

Angad (2nd) devised Gurmukhi script. Amar Das (3rd) institutionalised langar, set up manjis, opposed sati and purdah; Akbar visited him. Ram Das (4th) founded Amritsar (land from Akbar) and the Harmandir sarovar, started the masand system. The Guruship became hereditary after him.
Arjan Dev (5th)

Compiled the Adi Granth (1604) with verses of Gurus, Kabir, Ravidas, Farid. Completed the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) in 1604, founded Tarn Taran and Kartarpur (Jalandhar). Executed in 1606 under Jahangir (supporting Khusrau). Considered the first martyr.
Hargobind and Tegh Bahadur

Hargobind (6th) wore two swords ( miri and piri ), built the Akal Takht , fought Mughal forces. Har Rai (7th) and Har Krishan (8th; child Guru). Tegh Bahadur (9th) founded Anandpur Sahib; he was executed at Delhi in 1675 under Aurangzeb for defending Kashmiri Pandits’ right to worship (Gurdwara Sis Ganj).
The ten Gurus
Guru Gobind Singh (10th)

On Baisakhi 1699 at Anandpur he founded the Khalsa with the Panj Pyare and the Five Ks (kesh, kangha, kara, kirpan, kachera). Surname Singh and Kaur. Battles at Bhangani and Chamkaur. Composed the Dasam Granth; ended the line of living Gurus, declaring the Guru Granth Sahib to be Guru (1708, Nanded). Banda Singh Bahadur led the next phase.
After the Gurus

Banda Singh Bahadur (1708 to 1716) captured Sirhind. Misls (12 confederacies) and then Maharaja Ranjit Singh (r. 1799 to 1839) built the Sikh Empire from Lahore, with the Anglo-Sikh wars (1845–46; 1848–49) ending it. The Singh Sabha (1873) and Akali movement (Gurdwara Reform Act, 1925; SGPC) followed.
Faith or politics?

W. H. McLeod argued that early Sikhism was a movement of the Sant tradition (like Kabir), that later became militant. Others (Harbans Singh) stress continuity of spiritual-political thought from Nanak. The sources for the early period are also debated.
Today

The Kartarpur Corridor (Gurdaspur to Pakistan’s Kartarpur Sahib) opened in November 2019 for Guru Nanak’s 550th birth anniversary. Veer Bal Diwas is observed on 26 December for the Sahibzade. The Golden Temple’s langar serves tens of thousands daily. Punjabi in Gurmukhi is a constitutional language.
The Khalsa and the Adi Granth

The Sikh Gurus built a faith with its own scripture, shared kitchen and community. Guru Nanak began it in the late 15th century. The community grew into a political force by the 1700s. A worked case: the Adi Granth. Guru Arjan Dev compiled the Adi Granth in 1604 and installed it at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar. The text has hymns by the Gurus and by Bhakti and Sufi saints, such as Kabir and Farid. A sharp distinction: the Khalsa. In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa at Anandpur, on Vaisakhi. Members took a shared identity and vows. The Khalsa turned the community into a disciplined body. The Guru Granth Sahib. After Guru Gobind Singh, Sikhs regard the Guru Granth Sahib as the eternal Guru. No living person succeeded him as Guru. Exam trap. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, was executed in Delhi in 1675. Do not mix up the order of the Gurus. How it is asked. Prelims: the Adi Granth, the Khalsa and Guru Nanak’s teachings. Mains: discuss the role of the Sikh Gurus in shaping Sikh identity and politics.
How to answer
“Evolution of the Sikh religion from Nanak to Gobind Singh.” Prelims: Arjan, Adi Granth, Khalsa 1699, Five Ks, Akal Takht. Mains: Relationship of Sikh Gurus and Mughals.
Bhakti and Sufi Traditions
Faith that crossed boundaries
Bhakti and Sufism are the main strands of medieval religious life. They shaped language, music and social ideas. UPSC asks for saints, teachings and effects.
Origins of Bhakti

Bhakti (devotion) began in the south with the Alvars (Vishnu) and Nayanars (Shiva), between the 6th and 9th centuries, who sang in Tamil and welcomed women and low castes (Andal, Karaikkal Ammaiyar). Texts: Nalayira Divya Prabandham , Tevaram . Later: Shankara’s Advaita (8th c.), Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita, 11th to 12th c.), Madhva (Dvaita), Basavanna’s Lingayat movement (Karnataka, 12th c.; Anubhava Mandapa).
Bhakti in the north

Ramananda (14th to 15th c.): Rama bhakti; disciples include Kabir and Ravidas. Kabir : nirguna God, attacked idol worship and caste; Bijak. Guru Nanak : one God, equality, langar , sangat . Chaitanya (Bengal): Krishna bhakti, kirtan . Tulsidas ( Ramcharitmanas ), Surdas , Mirabai , Raskhan . Vallabhacharya (Pushtimarga).
Maharashtra and the east

Varkari tradition : Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram, Janabai; Pandharpur and Vitthal. Sankaradeva (Assam, Ekasarana dharma ), Shrimanta Sankardeva ’s Namghar and Borgeet . Others: Narsi Mehta (Gujarat), Chandidas (Bengal), Annamacharya (Andhra). Many saints came from low castes and used the vernacular.
Sufism

Sufism is the mystical stream of Islam, stressing love and union with God. Orders ( silsilas ): Chishti (Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer; Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi; Baba Farid), Suhrawardi (Multan, Bahauddin Zakariya), Qadiri , Naqshbandi (Sirhindi, who opposed Akbar’s liberalism). Practices: khanqah , sama (music), langar . Chishtis kept away from the state; Suhrawardis accepted it.
Common ground and expression

Both movements used local languages: Kabir and Tulsi in Hindi, Dnyaneshwar in Marathi, Sufis in Dakhni and Hindavi (Amir Khusrau, Baba Farid in Punjabi). The Chishtis of Ajmer and Delhi attracted Hindu and Muslim devotees. Sufi poets such as Jayasi ( Padmavat ) and Rahim. Qawwali and bhajan, Kabir panth and Sikhism came from them. Both rejected rigid orthodoxy.
Social impact

They challenged caste, ritual and priestly control; spread vernacular literature; gave women a voice (Mirabai, Lalla Ded). They brought communities closer and helped shape the ganga-jamuni tehzeeb . Yet they did not abolish caste; many movements later formed new sects or castes. Akbar’s sulh-i-kul was nurtured in this air.
Social revolt or spiritual reform?

Historians (Satish Chandra, Irfan Habib) see Bhakti as a response to a changing society and urban craft groups; Marxists tied it to peasants and artisans. Others (Romila Thapar) view it as a religious expression within a plural society. Scholars debate the term “movement”, as the saints were not organised. On Sufis, Richard Eaton ( Sufis of Bijapur ) studies state ties.
Why it matters today

Kabir’s and Mirabai’s verses are in school books and music. The dargah of Ajmer, with a huge urs, draws all faiths. Pandharpur’s wari draws lakhs. Discussion on communal harmony cites these traditions; recent controversies over dargahs and temples revisit it. The Sikh langar became a symbol of free community kitchens worldwide.
Sufi silsilas and Bhakti roots

Sufi orders, called silsilas, were lineages of teachers. Each had its own style, from quiet prayer to public music. The Chishti order was the most influential in India. A worked case: the Chishtis. Moinuddin Chishti settled in Ajmer. Nizamuddin Auliya led a large community in Delhi. Their khanqahs, or hospices, welcomed people of many faiths. Qawwali, sung at their shrines, became a mark of the tradition. A sharp distinction: Bhakti and Sufism. Bhakti stressed devotion to a personal god, often through songs in local languages. Sufism stressed love of God and inner experience. Both moved beyond ritual, but their roots differed. Exam trap. Bhakti was not a single movement. It was a set of many regional traditions, from Kabir in the north to Basava in Karnataka. Do not treat it as one religion. A famous debate. Some historians see Bhakti as social revolt. Others see spiritual reform. Much of the evidence comes from later lives of saints, so read it with care. How it is asked. Prelims: Chishti and Suhrawardi orders, Qawwali and Bhakti traditions. Mains: discuss the role of the Bhakti and Sufi movements in medieval Indian society.
How to answer

“Bhakti and Sufi movements promoted social harmony. Discuss.” “Compare the teachings of Kabir and Guru Nanak.” Prelims tip: Alvars = Vishnu; Nayanars = Shiva; Ramanuja = Vishishtadvaita; Basavanna = Lingayat; Chishti = Ajmer, Nizamuddin; Suhrawardi = Multan.
Bhakti Saints in Depth
Individual saints, not just ideas

The existing lesson covers the movement. Here we learn each saint, region and message , because Prelims matches names to ideas. The Bhakti movement spread from the Tamil south in a long chain of saints.
The Tamil roots

Alvars (12 Vaishnava poets; Andal, Nammalvar, Periyalvar), whose verses are compiled in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham . Nayanars (63 Shaiva saints; Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar, Manikkavachakar), compiled in the Tirumurai by Nambiyandar Nambi. Both rejected caste barriers and used Tamil.
Acharyas and philosophy

Shankara (Advaita, 8th century, Kaladi). Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita, 11th to 12th century; Sri Bhashya). Madhva (Dvaita, Udupi). Nimbarka (Dvaitadvaita), Vallabhacharya (Pushtimarg, Shuddhadvaita). Ramananda (Varanasi, 14th century) took Bhakti north, with disciples including Kabir, Ravidas and Sena the barber.
Nirguna saints

Kabir (15th century; Bijak, Sakhi, Ramaini): formless God, rejected idol worship and caste, both Hindu and Muslim ritual; weaver of Varanasi. Guru Nanak and Dadu Dayal (Rajasthan). Ravidas (cobbler, Varanasi; Mirabai’s guru in tradition). Languages were Hindi dialects. Compiled in the Granth.
Regional Bhakti voices
Saguna saints in the north

Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas, Awadhi, c. 1574), Surdas (Sur Sagar, Braj, Krishna), Mirabai (Krishna devotee, Mewar), Chaitanya (Bengal, kirtan, Gaudiya Vaishnavism), Narsinh Mehta (Gujarat, “Vaishnav Jan To”). Sankaradeva (Assam) founded Ek Sarana Dharma and the sattra institution, plus Borgeet and Ankia Naat.
Maharashtra and Karnataka

Dnyaneshwar (Dnyaneshwari, a Marathi commentary on the Gita, 1290), Namdev , Eknath , Tukaram (abhangas), Chokhamela and Janabai: Varkari panth centred on Vitthala of Pandharpur . Basavanna (12th century, Kalyana) founded Veerashaivism with vachanas , the Anubhava Mantapa, rejecting caste and ritual.
Social revolution or accommodation?

Some see Bhakti as a challenge to caste and Brahmin ritual (Kabir, Ravidas). Others, like Romila Thapar, see it as often absorbed into the existing structure; many saints still accepted varna. Irfan Habib links it to artisan and peasant protest against feudal order. Interaction with Sufism is another thread.
Today

Pandharpur’s Ashadhi Wari pilgrimage draws lakhs of Warkaris every year. Sant Kabir Jayanti and Tulsi Jayanti are celebrated. Bhakti poetry shaped modern Hindi, Marathi and Assamese. The Statue of Equality (216 ft, Hyderabad, 2022) honours Ramanuja.
Kabir, Mirabai and Tukaram

Bhakti saints wrote in local languages so that common people could follow. Their poems are still sung. Each saint had a distinct voice and place. A worked case: Kabir. Kabir, a weaver, rejected ritual and idol worship. He spoke of one formless God, which is the nirguna idea. His couplets, called dohas, are in the Adi Granth. His teaching cut across Hindu and Muslim lines. Mirabai. A Rajput princess who sang to Krishna and rejected the rules of the court. Her songs in Braj and Rajasthani are still sung today. She is a saguna saint, one who worships a god with form. Tukaram. A Maharashtrian saint who wrote abhangs, short devotional verses, to the god Vitthala of Pandharpur. His verses gave ordinary people a voice. Exam trap. Kabir is nirguna, with a formless God. Tulsidas and Surdas are saguna, with a god who has form. Do not put them in the wrong group. Why it matters. The saints show how religion could speak in everyday language, and this shaped later regional literature. How it is asked. Prelims: nirguna vs saguna saints, and the language or region of each. Mains: examine the social message of the Bhakti saints.
How to answer
“Bhakti saints promoted social equality. Examine.” “Compare Kabir and Nanak.” Prelims: Alvars vs Nayanars, Ramananda’s disciples, Sankaradeva, Basavanna.
Temple Architecture: Nagara, Dravida, Vesara
Stone as history
Temples are the best-preserved record of Indian kings, faith and craft. UPSC asks for style features, dynasties and examples, often with a UNESCO angle.
Parts of a temple

Garbhagriha (sanctum), mandapa (hall), shikhara or vimana (tower), antarala (vestibule), amalaka (ribbed disc on Nagara tower), kalasha (finial). Early Gupta temples (Deogarh Dashavatara, Bhitargaon brick temple) set the pattern. The three broad styles are described in the Vastu texts: Nagara (north), Dravida (south), Vesara (Deccan mix).
Nagara style

Found from the Himalayas to the Vindhyas. Features: a curved shikhara ( rekha-deula or latina type), temple on a raised platform, no boundary wall or large gateway. Sub-schools: Odisha (Lingaraja, Bhubaneswar; Konark Sun Temple; Jagannath, Puri; deul and jagamohana), Khajuraho (Chandela, Kandariya Mahadeva, c. 1000 CE; panchayatana plan), Solanki (Modhera Sun Temple, Gujarat, 1026), Dilwara Jain temples (Mount Abu).
Dravida style

The tower is a stepped pyramid, vimana , with a rectangular compound wall and a large gopuram at the gateway. A water tank and pillared halls are common. Dynasties: Pallavas (Mahabalipuram Shore Temple, Kanchi Kailasanatha), Cholas (Brihadisvara, Thanjavur, built by Rajaraja I about 1010 CE; Gangaikonda Cholapuram; Airavatesvara, Darasuram), Pandyas and Nayakas (Madurai Meenakshi, large gopurams).
Vesara and other styles

Vesara is the mixed style of the Deccan. Chalukyas of Badami and Aihole (Durga temple, Virupaksha at Pattadakal), Rashtrakutas (Kailasa at Ellora, carved from one rock under Krishna I), Hoysalas (Belur, Halebid, Somnathpur; star-shaped plan on a platform, soapstone, called jagati ). Others: Kashmir (Martand Sun Temple, Karkota), Himachal (wooden temples), Kerala (sloping roofs), Assam (Kamakhya).
Rock-cut and monolithic

Barabar caves (Mauryan, polished). Kanheri, Karle. Elephanta (Shiva, Maharashtra). The Kailasa temple at Ellora is carved top down from a single rock. Pallava monolithic rathas at Mahabalipuram (Narasimhavarman I Mamalla). Ajanta and Ellora combine Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves.
How strict are the labels?

The Nagara-Dravida-Vesara scheme is helpful but not sharp: Odisha and Khajuraho differ from each other, and the Deccan mixed both. Scholars such as Adam Hardy speak of a “Karnata Dravida” tradition. Still, for exams, learn the three types and exceptions.
Why it matters today

Great Living Chola Temples (Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, Darasuram), Khajuraho, Konark, Mahabalipuram, Pattadakal, Hampi and the Hoysala temples are UNESCO World Heritage sites (the Hoysala group was added in 2023). The Ram temple at Ayodhya (consecrated January 2024) is built in the Nagara style. Temple economy and the HR&CE laws in states raise legal debates.
Reading a temple’s shape

Indian temples are often sorted into Nagara (north), Dravida (south) and Vesara (mixed). The name points to the region. Each style has its own tower. In the north it is the shikhara, and in the south it is the vimana. A worked case: Kandariya Mahadeva. This Chandela temple at Khajuraho, built in the early 11th century, is a fine Nagara temple. Its tower rises in a curve and is packed with carved figures. Inside, the garbhagriha is the inner sanctum, and the mandapa is the hall before it. A sharp distinction: shikhara and vimana. The Nagara shikhara is a curved tower that rises in one smooth line. The Dravida vimana is a stepped pyramid. Learn the difference by the outline. Rock-cut and monolith. Kailasanatha at Ellora in Maharashtra is carved from one hill, from the top down. It is a Rashtrakuta temple of the 8th century. It shows the same skill used for rock and structure. Exam trap. The Brihadeeswarar at Thanjavur is a Dravida temple. Khajuraho is Nagara. Do not switch them. How it is asked. Prelims: match a temple with its style, such as Khajuraho with Nagara. Mains: examine the regional styles of Indian temple architecture.
How to answer

“Distinguish between Nagara and Dravida architecture.” Use a two-column table. “Chola temple architecture was a mirror of imperial power.” Prelims tip: gopuram = Dravida; shikhara with amalaka = Nagara; star plan = Hoysala; Kailasa at Ellora = Rashtrakuta.
Buddhist, Indo-Islamic and Colonial Architecture
Layers of one building tradition
Stupas, mosques, forts and Victorian railway stations are all part of the same story. UPSC wants you to date them and to name the style.
Buddhist architecture

Stupa : relic mound. Parts: anda (dome), harmika , chhatra , vedika , torana . Sanchi (Ashoka, later enlarged under Shungas and Satavahanas; torana gates), Bharhut, Amaravati, Sarnath (Dhamek). Chaityas (prayer halls) and viharas (monasteries): Karle chaitya, Ajanta, Bhaja. Ashokan pillars with lion capitals (Sarnath; national emblem).
Delhi Sultanate architecture

Introduced the arch, dome, minaret and lime mortar, using the true arch . Phases: Slave (Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, Qutb Minar, Adhai Din ka Jhonpra, Ajmer), Khalji (Alai Darwaza, Siri), Tughlaq (Tughlaqabad; sloping walls, Firozshah Kotla), Sayyid-Lodi (octagonal tombs, Lodi Garden). Provincial: Jaunpur (Atala Masjid), Gujarat (Jama Masjid, Ahmedabad; Sidi Saiyyed jali), Bengal, Malwa (Hoshang Shah’s tomb), Bijapur (Gol Gumbaz, with a very large dome).
Mughal architecture

Babur : gardens. Humayun’s tomb (Delhi, 1560s, Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas; first garden-tomb, charbagh). Akbar : Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri (Buland Darwaza, Jodha Bai palace, Panch Mahal; red sandstone), Akbar’s tomb at Sikandra. Jahangir : Itimad-ud-daula (Nur Jahan; first use of white marble and pietra dura ). Shah Jahan : Taj Mahal (1632 to 1653, Ustad Ahmad Lahori), Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Moti Masjid. Aurangzeb : Bibi ka Maqbara, Badshahi Mosque, Lahore.
Regional and Rajput forts

Rajput forts: Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Amber, Jaisalmer, Mehrangarh. Hill Forts of Rajasthan are UNESCO sites (2013). Deccan: Golconda, Daulatabad. Vijayanagara: Hampi (Vittala temple stone chariot; Lotus Mahal; Indo-Islamic mix). Sikh: Golden Temple, Amritsar (Guru Arjan Dev; Harmandir Sahib). The Sultanate and Mughal forms blended with local craft: the chhatri , jharokha and jali are Indian elements.
Colonial architecture

Early : Portuguese and French churches (Basilica of Bom Jesus, Goa), Danish Tranquebar. Classical : Fort William (Calcutta), Government House. Indo-Saracenic : Gateway of India, Victoria Memorial, Madras High Court (Robert Chisholm, F. W. Stevens). Gothic : Victoria Terminus (Mumbai), University of Mumbai. Imperial Delhi : Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker, New Delhi (1911 to 1931), Rashtrapati Bhavan, India Gate.
Modern after 1947

Le Corbusier’s Chandigarh (Capitol Complex is a UNESCO site since 2016); Louis Kahn (IIM Ahmedabad); Charles Correa (Gandhi Smarak, Jawahar Kala Kendra); Laurie Baker’s low-cost homes; B. V. Doshi (Pritzker 2018). The new Parliament building was inaugurated in May 2023 as part of the Central Vista project.
Was Indo-Saracenic respectful or political?

Thomas Metcalf ( An Imperial Vision , 1989) argued that Indo-Saracenic was a style of empire: British rulers used Indian forms to show themselves as heirs to Mughals. Others stress craftsmanship by Indian workers and the hybrid creativity. The Central Vista debate echoes the old question of how power uses architecture.
Why it matters today

The Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Qutb Minar, Humayun’s Tomb, Sanchi, Rani ki Vav (Gujarat), Victorian Gothic and Art Deco of Mumbai (2018) and Ahmedabad (2017, India’s first World Heritage City) show a living urban heritage. Conservation, ASI protected monuments and the Ancient Monuments Act 1958 are all in the news.
One building tradition, many layers

India’s building history is layered. Buddhist, Sultanate, Mughal, Rajput and colonial styles often stand side by side in one city. Each layer tells a story about power and patrons. A worked case: the Qutb Minar. The Qutb complex in Delhi was begun by Qutb-ud-din Aibak in 1192. The tower was finished by his successors. The complex has an iron pillar that has resisted rust for many centuries. A sharp distinction: Indo-Saracenic. The Victoria Memorial in Kolkata, opened in 1921, mixes Mughal-style domes with a European marble style. It was built by the British in honour of Queen Victoria. The style is often called Indo-Saracenic. Buddhist architecture. Stupas, chaityas and viharas show the Buddhist building tradition. Sanchi and the Ajanta caves are famous examples. The caves were cut into rock, with prayer halls and monks’ rooms. Exam trap. Do not say that all Indo-Islamic buildings were meant to show power. Many were tombs, mosques or hospices, each with its own purpose. How it is asked. Prelims: the Qutb Minar, the Victoria Memorial and Sanchi, matched with their periods. Mains: examine the blend of Indian and foreign styles in Indian architecture.
How to answer

“Mughal architecture synthesised Persian and Indian elements. Discuss.” “Indo-Saracenic architecture—what and why?” Prelims tip: Humayun’s tomb (charbagh), Itimad-ud-daula (pietra dura), Buland Darwaza (Akbar), Gol Gumbaz (Bijapur), Delhi Gate and India Gate (Lutyens).
Sculpture: Mauryan to Chola Bronzes
Stone and metal that speak
Each period of Indian sculpture has a signature look. Prelims asks you to match a school with its features and its material.
Indus and Mauryan

Harappan : bearded priest (steatite), dancing girl (bronze, lost-wax), seals. Mauryan : polished sandstone, Chunar. Court art: Ashokan pillars and lion capital from Sarnath; Didarganj Yakshi; Dhauli elephant. Folk art: Parkham Yaksha (Mathura), Yakshis and Yakshas.
Post-Mauryan schools

Gandhara (Kushana): Greco-Roman influence, Buddha with wavy hair, drapery, grey schist. Mathura : indigenous, red sandstone, first Buddha figures as well as Jain and Hindu figures; Kanishka’s headless statue. Amaravati (Satavahana): white marble, narrative friezes with the body shown as flowing. Bharhut and Sanchi reliefs show aniconic Buddha (wheel, tree, footprints).
Gupta and post-Gupta

Classical grace and calm. Sarnath Buddha in teaching pose ( dharmachakra mudra ); Mathura standing Buddha; Sultanganj copper Buddha. Hindu icons: Vishnu at Deogarh, Varaha at Udayagiri. After the Guptas: Pala (Bengal, black basalt, bronze at Nalanda), Pratihara and Chandela.
Pallava and Chalukya sculpture

Mahabalipuram: Descent of the Ganga (Arjuna’s Penance) , a huge relief on a rock face; Mahishasuramardini cave. Elephanta (Trimurti, Shiva). Badami and Aihole (Chalukya). Ellora: Ravana shaking Kailasa. Natural movement and balance in all these.
Chola bronzes

Cast by the lost-wax (cire perdue) method, an old Indian process. A clay model is covered in wax, then in clay again, wax is melted out, and metal is poured in. The Cholas (9th to 13th centuries) made the most famous bronzes: Nataraja (Shiva as cosmic dancer, ring of flames), Shiva as Ardhanarishvara, Sivakami, Rama, Sita, Hanuman, Parvati. The Swamimalai artisans (the sthapathis ) still follow the old method.
Reading a Nataraja

The raised right hand holds the damaru (creation), the left holds fire (destruction). Another right hand makes abhaya (fear not); the left points to the raised foot (release). He dances on the dwarf Apasmara , the demon of ignorance. The ring of fire is the cosmos. The image became a symbol of Indian art; a Nataraja statue stands at CERN, Geneva (2004).
Gandhara: borrowed or reborn?

Western scholars once called it “Greco-Buddhist” and the high point of Indian Buddhist art. Indian nationalists such as Coomaraswamy argued the Mathura school was truly Indian and older in iconography. Today most see both as parallel responses to patronage in the Kushana world. For exams: keep the contrasts clear.
Why it matters today

Stolen idols are returning: Nataraja and other bronzes are repatriated by US and UK museums. The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972 governs trade. Chola bronzes are among India’s GI-protected craft (Swamimalai bronze icons). Nataraja is the logo of the Indian government’s cultural bodies.
Mauryan stone and Chola bronze

Indian sculpture moved from stone pillars to clay, stone and metal figures. The style changed by region, and the patrons changed too. A worked case: the Chola bronze. Chola bronzes were often made by the lost-wax method. A wax model was covered in clay, the wax was melted out, and molten metal filled the space. The Nataraja, Shiva as the dancing king, is the best-known bronze. A sharp distinction: Gandhara and Mathura. Gandhara art, in the north-west, shows the Buddha with Greek-style drapery and features. Mathura art, in the north, is more Indian in form and used red sandstone. Both were made in the Kushana period. Exam trap. Do not say that Gandhara art came from India alone or from Greece alone. Scholars see a blend of local and Greco-Roman ideas. The Gupta calm. Gupta sculpture is calm and balanced, with a simple halo. The Sarnath Buddha is a famous example of this classical style. How it is asked. Prelims: the lost-wax method, Gandhara vs Mathura, and the Nataraja. Mains: discuss the evolution of Indian sculpture and its regional schools.
How to answer

“Compare the Gandhara and Mathura schools.” Use a table: patron, material, influence, features. “Chola bronzes represent the height of Indian metal sculpture.” Prelims tip: Gandhara = grey schist, Hellenistic; Mathura = red sandstone, indigenous; Amaravati = white marble; lost-wax = Chola and Harappan.
Painting: Ajanta to the Miniature Schools
Colour and story on walls and paper
Painting questions in Prelims ask for school, region and theme. In Mains they ask about Mughal and Rajput contrast or Company paintings.
Prehistoric and early

Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh), rock paintings of the Stone Age, a UNESCO site (2003). Ajanta (Maharashtra), 2nd century BCE to c. 480 CE: Buddhist cave murals. Fresco secco technique. Themes: Jataka tales, Padmapani and Vajrapani, the Mother and Child panel. Bagh caves (Madhya Pradesh). Sittanavasal (Jain, Tamil Nadu). Ellora has few paintings.
Pala, Jain and Pre-Mughal

Pala (Buddhist palm-leaf manuscripts of Nalanda, Vikramashila). Jain western Indian manuscripts (Kalpasutra, Gujarat), with bold lines and large eyes, often silver and gold ink. Sultanate : Persian influence, e.g. Nimatnama. Vijayanagara : Lepakshi murals.
Mughal painting

Rooted in Persian miniature. Humayun brought Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd as-Samad. Akbar : Hamzanama ; Razmnama ; Daswanth, Basawan. Jahangir : naturalism, portraits, birds and flowers; Ustad Mansur (falcons, flowers); Bishandas. Shah Jahan : refined, formal. Aurangzeb : court patronage fell; artists left for provincial courts. Features: realism, perspective, portraits, durbar scenes, borders.
Rajasthani and Pahari schools

Rajasthani (Mewar, Bundi, Kishangarh, Jaipur, Marwar): bold colours, Ragamala, Krishna Lila, Gita Govinda. Kishangarh: Bani Thani (Nihal Chand), long eyes and slender faces. Pahari (Basohli, Guler, Kangra): soft colours, lyrical, Radha-Krishna; Kangra painting under Raja Sansar Chand, 18th century; Nainsukh of Guler. Basohli: bold and early (17th century).
Deccan, Company and modern

Deccani : Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmednagar; rich colours, Ragamala. Company school (late 18th century): Indian artists for British patrons, with natural history subjects; Patna Kalam. Raja Ravi Varma : oleo-prints, Hindu gods in realistic European style. Bengal School (Abanindranath Tagore, Bharat Mata ); Nandalal Bose (Constitution illustrations); Amrita Sher-Gil; Progressive Artists’ Group, 1947 (Souza, Husain, Raza).
Folk paintings

Madhubani (Bihar, GI), Warli (Maharashtra, geometric on mud walls), Pattachitra (Odisha, West Bengal), Kalamkari (Andhra, pen work), Tanjore, Phad (Rajasthan scroll), Gond, Kalighat, Pithora, Cheriyal scrolls. Many have GI tags. Padma awards often go to these artists (e.g. Jivya Soma Mashe, Warli).
Who gets credit: patron or painter?

Court painting names painters rarely; the studio, karkhana , worked under a patron. Mughal paintings carried the emperor’s taste. The Bengal School turned to Asian spiritual tradition as an anti-colonial act, while Ravi Varma’s mass prints shaped popular religion. Debate: nationalism versus realism.
Why it matters today

Madhubani on railway stations and the Warli wall art on public buildings link craft to livelihood schemes. GI tags protect makers. The National Gallery of Modern Art (Delhi, 1954) and National Museum hold masterpieces. The “One District One Product” scheme promotes such crafts.
Why the Ajanta murals were painted in phases

The Ajanta caves in Maharashtra were carved over several centuries. Their murals are not from one time. Scholars usually describe two main phases of painting. The earlier phase belongs to the period of the Satavahana era, and the later, richer phase to the Vakataka period, roughly the fifth century. The murals show the Buddha's past lives, the Jataka tales, and scenes of palace life. The paintings were made on a plaster surface, which was smoothed and then painted. Where paint went on wet plaster it is called fresco buono. Where it went on dry plaster it is called fresco secco, and Ajanta uses that method for many parts. Why the caves matter for later art Ajanta shows how Indian painting used line, colour and gesture to tell a story. Later Pala manuscripts, Jain paintings and Rajput schools inherited these habits. A student who knows Ajanta can see the roots of later Indian painting. Exam trap: fresco secco is not the same as fresco buono. The first is painting on dry plaster, and the second is painting on wet plaster. Many quiz questions ask which is which. How it is asked: Prelims asks which site has Buddhist cave murals or what fresco buono means. Mains asks how Ajanta shows the link between religion, patronage and the growth of Indian painting.
How to answer

“Mughal and Rajput painting: similarities and differences.” “Ajanta paintings in the history of Indian art.” Prelims tip: Bani Thani = Kishangarh; Hamzanama = Akbar; Kangra = Pahari; Patna Kalam = Company school; Bhimbetka = prehistoric; Ajanta = fresco secco, Buddhist.
Classical and Folk Dances
Dance is a favourite Prelims topic
Questions ask which dance belongs to which state, who the exponents are, and what is classical. The Natya Shastra and the Sangeet Natak Akademi are the key reference points.
What makes a dance classical

The Natya Shastra of Bharata (c. 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE) gives the base: nritta (pure dance), nritya (expressive dance), natya (drama); abhinaya (expression) and rasa (mood). The Sangeet Natak Akademi (1953) recognises eight classical forms; the Ministry of Culture (2000) added Chhau in debate but does not list it. The commonly listed eight: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Kathakali, Sattriya, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam.
Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi

Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu): from Sadir of temple devadasis ; Tanjore Quartet (Chinnaiah, Ponniah, Sivanandam, Vadivelu). Alarippu , jatiswaram , varnam , tillana . Revived by E. Krishna Iyer and Rukmini Devi Arundale (Kalakshetra, 1936). Cut off the “devadasi” tag. Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh): Siddhendra Yogi; originally male Brahmin troupes; tarangam (dance on a brass plate).
Kathak and Odissi

Kathak (north India): kathakars (storytellers); Persian influence under the Mughals; gharanas Jaipur, Lucknow, Banaras; tatkar , chakkars ; Birju Maharaj, Sitara Devi. Odissi (Odisha): temple maharis , Khandagiri-Udayagiri carvings; tribhanga posture; Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda ; Kelucharan Mohapatra.
Kathakali, Mohiniyattam, Sattriya, Manipuri

Kathakali (Kerala): elaborate make-up and costume; stories from the epics; mudras ; Vallathol revived it (Kerala Kalamandalam, 1930). Mohiniyattam (Kerala): female solo; lasya style; swaying movements. Sattriya (Assam): Sankardeva (15th century), monasteries ( sattras ); recognised in 2000. Manipuri : Vaishnava Raslila; soft, lyrical; costume kumil ; Ras Leela, Pung cholom.
Folk and tribal dance

Garba, Dandiya (Gujarat); Bhangra, Giddha (Punjab); Lavani, Koli (Maharashtra); Ghoomar, Kalbelia (Rajasthan, Kalbelia in UNESCO ICH list 2010). Bihu (Assam); Chhau (Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal; UNESCO 2010); Yakshagana (Karnataka); Theyyam (Kerala); Dollu Kunitha; Karakattam; Garadi; Nati (Himachal). Tribal: Ho, Santhal, Gond, Naga dances.
Institutions and honours

Sangeet Natak Akademi (1952 inaugurated, 1953 constituted), National School of Drama, Kalakshetra, Kerala Kalamandalam, Sangeet Natak Akademi Awards, Padma awards. UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: Kutiyattam (2008), Chhau (2010), Kalbelia (2010), Garba of Gujarat (inscribed December 2023).
Tradition or classicisation?

Historians such as Avanthi Meduri and Janet O’Shea examine how the 20th-century nationalist revival “classicised” Sadir by removing devadasis from the stage and promoting a respectable Brahmanical image. Critics say this erased hereditary women artists. Others credit Rukmini Devi with saving the art.
Why it matters today

Dance is soft power: ICCR and Indian missions send troupes abroad. Garba’s UNESCO listing, Yoga Day and Padma awards to folk artists show state support. Livelihood concerns of folk artists and the ban on dancing in public have been debated; Sangeet Natak Akademi offers pensions to senior artists.
Nritta, nritya and natya in one example

The Natya Shastra gives three parts of dance. Nritta is pure dance, with rhythm, footwork and body shapes that do not tell a story. Nritya adds meaning, through facial expression and hand gestures to show feeling. Natya is the wider art of drama, including the whole performance. A simple way to see it. Think of a dancer hearing a song about a monsoon. If she only moves her feet to the beat, she is doing nritta. If she uses her eyes and hands to show longing for rain, she is doing nritya. If the whole stage tells a story with actors and music, it is natya. What abhinaya adds Abhinaya is expression. It uses the face, eyes, hands and body to show emotion, called bhava. Classical dances such as Bharatanatyam and Odissi are known for their strong abhinaya, which is why they are often taught with the Natya Shastra as a base. Exam trap: a dance is classical not because it is old or famous. It follows a set grammar from a text, with defined postures, rhythm and training. Folk dances are community-based and do not follow such a grammar. How it is asked: Prelims asks what nritta and abhinaya mean, or which text is the base of classical dance. Mains asks how classical and folk dance keep India's cultural heritage alive and what threatens them today.
How to answer

“Classical dances of India reflect the diversity of regional culture. Discuss.” “Differences between Bharatanatyam and Kathak.” Prelims tip: Sattriya = Assam, Sankardeva; Kuchipudi = Andhra; Mohiniyattam = Kerala female; Odissi = Odisha, tribhanga; Chhau and Kalbelia = UNESCO lists.
Music and Theatre Traditions
Sound and stage
The split between Hindustani and Carnatic music, the gharanas and the lineage of folk theatre are staples of Prelims. Mains asks for cultural synthesis.
Roots and two streams

The Natya Shastra and later Sangita Ratnakara (Sharngadeva, 13th century) are textual roots. Music divides into Hindustani (north) and Carnatic (south) after the 13th to 14th century, with Persian influence in the north. Key concepts: raga (melodic frame), tala (rhythm), swara (note), shruti (microtone).
Hindustani music

Dhrupad : old, solemn; Man Singh Tomar of Gwalior; Tansen at Akbar’s court; Swami Haridas. Khayal : Amir Khusrau credited (disputed); Sultan Husain Sharqi; grew under Sadarang in Mohammad Shah’s time. Thumri, Tappa, Dadra, Ghazal : light forms. Gharanas : Gwalior, Agra, Kirana, Jaipur-Atrauli, Patiala, Rampur-Sahaswan. Instruments: sitar, sarod, santoor, tabla, shehnai. Ravi Shankar, Ali Akbar Khan, Bismillah Khan, Bhimsen Joshi.
Carnatic music

Foundation: Purandara Dasa (father of Carnatic music). The Trinity : Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, Shyama Shastri (18th century, Thanjavur). Forms: kriti , varnam , tillana , ragam-tanam-pallavi . Instruments: veena, mridangam, violin, ghatam, nadaswaram. M. S. Subbulakshmi (Bharat Ratna 1998), M. Balamuralikrishna. Melakarta system of 72 parent ragas (Venkatamakhin, 17th century; later reworked).
Other musical streams

Folk: Baul (Bengal), Bhatiyali , Pandavani (Chhattisgarh), Lavani , Alha . Devotional: Rabindra Sangeet, Qawwali (Sufi; Amir Khusrau), Abhangs (Maharashtra), Sufi kalam. Modern: film music and fusion. Bands and the Vande Mataram and Jana Gana Mana traditions run through all of them.
Sanskrit and classical theatre

Sanskrit drama: Bhasa, Kalidasa ( Abhijnana Shakuntalam ), Shudraka ( Mrichchhakatika ), Bhavabhuti, Vishakhadatta ( Mudrarakshasa ). Kutiyattam (Kerala), the only surviving Sanskrit theatre tradition, is a UNESCO Masterpiece (2001, listed ICH 2008). Performed by Chakyars and Nambiars .
Folk and modern theatre

Folk : Ramlila, Raslila, Nautanki (UP), Jatra (Bengal), Tamasha (Maharashtra), Bhavai (Gujarat), Yakshagana, Therukoothu, Pandavani, Bhand Pather (Kashmir), Ankia Naat (Assam). Modern : Parsi theatre; IPTA (1943); Habib Tanvir (Naya Theatre, Charandas Chor ); Utpal Dutt; Girish Karnad; Vijay Tendulkar ( Ghashiram Kotwal ); National School of Drama (1959, Ebrahim Alkazi).
Folk versus classical

Many treat folk and classical as high-low. Others see them as a loop: classical forms draw on folk tunes, folk forms borrow classical technique. The gharana system faces a debate on whether it is a closed lineage or an open school. The impact of recording and film on oral tradition also divides historians.
Why it matters today

Bismillah Khan, Ravi Shankar and Zakir Hussain made Indian music global. Tansen Samaroh (Gwalior), Sawai Gandharva festival and the Thyagaraja Aradhana keep tradition alive. Copyright in folk songs, GI claims and the Gurukul vs digital learning debate continue. Sangeet Natak Akademi and the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya preserve the arts.
Why Hindustani and Carnatic split

Indian music once shared many ideas. The split into a northern Hindustani style and a southern Carnatic style came gradually, in the period from about the 13th to the 16th century. Political courts, Persian and Sufi influences, and regional patronage all played a part. Both styles use raga , a set of notes with rules for mood and time, and tala , the rhythmic cycle. The difference lies in how they are shaped. Hindustani music has a stronger improvisation tradition within a raga. Carnatic music has a larger body of composed pieces, such as the kriti, which the performer adds to within set rules. Two ways to hear the difference A Hindustani khayal singer often takes a long time to develop a raga slowly. A Carnatic concert often moves through a series of composed kritis, each with a clear theme. Both are classical, but their structure and training differ. Exam trap: Carnatic is not only temple music. The Trinity of Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar and Shyama Shastri were all active in the eighteenth century in Thanjavur, and they wrote mostly devotional songs for concerts. How it is asked: Prelims asks which style uses kriti or which composers form the Carnatic Trinity. Mains asks how music traditions reflect the mix of religion, courts and regional life in India.
How to answer

“Compare Hindustani and Carnatic music.” “Folk theatre as a medium of social change.” Prelims tip: Trinity = Tyagaraja, Dikshitar, Shyama Shastri; Purandara Dasa = father of Carnatic; dhrupad = Man Singh Tomar; Kutiyattam = Kerala, UNESCO.
Indian Literature and Schools of Philosophy
The ideas behind the art
UPSC asks about Vedic texts, Buddhist canon, Sangam works, and the six schools of philosophy. This is high-yield theory with simple pairings.
Vedic and Sanskrit literature

Vedas : Rig, Sama, Yajur, Atharva; Brahmanas , Aranyakas , Upanishads (Vedanta). Epics : Ramayana (Valmiki), Mahabharata (Vyasa; Bhagavad Gita in the Bhishma Parva). Puranas . Classical : Kalidasa ( Meghaduta , Raghuvamsha ), Banabhatta ( Harshacharita ), Kalhana ( Rajatarangini , c. 1148, Kashmir), Panini ( Ashtadhyayi ), Kautilya ( Arthashastra ), Bharata (Natya Shastra).
Pali, Prakrit and Tamil

Buddhist : Tripitaka (Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma) in Pali; Jataka ; Dipavamsa , Mahavamsa (Sri Lanka). Jain : Agamas in Ardha-Magadhi. Sangam (Tamil): Tolkappiyam , Ettuthokai , Pattuppattu ; epics Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal) and Manimekalai (Sattanar); Tirukkural (Tiruvalluvar).
Medieval and regional

Tamil Bhakti hymns: Tevaram , Nalayira Divya Prabandham . Kannada: Pampa. Marathi: Dnyaneshwar’s Dnyaneshwari . Bengali: Chandidas, Chaitanya Charitamrita . Hindi: Kabir, Tulsidas ( Ramcharitmanas ), Surdas, Malik Muhammad Jayasi ( Padmavat ). Persian: Amir Khusrau, Abul Fazl ( Akbarnama , Ain-i-Akbari ), Babur’s Baburnama . Urdu: Mir, Ghalib.
Modern literature

Bankim Chandra ( Anandamath , 1882; Vande Mataram ), Tagore ( Gitanjali ; Nobel 1913), Premchand, Subramania Bharati, Mahadevi Varma, Sarat Chandra. Jnanpith Award (since 1965; first to G. Sankara Kurup). Sahitya Akademi Award (1954). The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages; classical language status given to Tamil (2004), Sanskrit (2005), Telugu and Kannada (2008), Malayalam (2013), Odia (2014), and Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali (October 2024).
Orthodox schools (astika)

Accept the Vedas. Six darshanas : Nyaya (Gautama, logic), Vaisheshika (Kanada, atomism), Sankhya (Kapila, dualism of purusha and prakriti ), Yoga (Patanjali, Yoga Sutras ), Mimamsa (Jaimini, ritual), Vedanta (Badarayana; Shankara’s Advaita, Ramanuja’s Vishishtadvaita, Madhva’s Dvaita).
Heterodox schools (nastika)

Buddhism : Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, anatta ; schools Theravada, Mahayana (Nagarjuna, Madhyamika; Asanga, Yogachara), Vajrayana. Jainism : Mahavira, 24 Tirthankaras, anekantavada , syadvada , five vows; Svetambara and Digambara. Charvaka (Lokayata): materialism; only perception is knowledge. Ajivika : fatalism, Makkhali Gosala.
Was Indian philosophy only religion?

Scholars like Debiprasad Chattopadhyaya ( Lokayata , 1959) stress the materialist strand. Amartya Sen in The Argumentative Indian (2005) shows a long tradition of public debate and dissent. Orientalists tended to present India as only mystical; recent writers show logic, science and politics (Arthashastra) as equally old.
Why it matters today

Classical language status brings funds for chairs and centres: in October 2024 five more languages were added, making 11. Yoga was inscribed by UNESCO in 2016 (ICH). Ideas of ahimsa and anekanta shaped Gandhi and today’s ideas of pluralism. The Constitution’s Eighth Schedule and Article 351 on Hindi tie to this literary heritage.
Six orthodox schools and a debate

Indian philosophy was a long debate. The orthodox schools, called astika, accept the authority of the Vedas. There are six classical systems, called darshanas, and each answers the question of how we know and what the self is in its own way. Nyaya, from Gautama, is the logic school. Vaisheshika, from Kanada, is the school of atoms and categories. Sankhya, from Kapila, splits reality into purusha, the self, and prakriti, nature. Yoga, from Patanjali, gives the path of practice. Mimamsa, from Jaimini, studies Vedic ritual. Vedanta, from Badarayana and later Shankara, explores the unity of self and ultimate reality. Heterodox schools Buddhism and Jainism are heterodox, or nastika, because they do not treat the Vedas as final authority. Buddhism teaches the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. Jainism stresses non-violence, or ahimsa, and the Tirthankaras. Exam trap: nastika does not mean atheist. It means the school does not accept Vedic authority. Some Buddhist and Jain thinkers still discussed the nature of the self in detail. How it is asked: Prelims asks which school founded the Nyaya logic or which schools are orthodox or heterodox. Mains asks how Indian philosophical debate shaped ethics, logic and social thought.
How to answer

“Discuss the contribution of the six schools of Indian philosophy.” “Indian philosophy is more than religion. Comment.” Prelims tip: Rajatarangini = Kalhana; Silappadikaram = Ilango Adigal; Sankhya = Kapila; Vaisheshika = Kanada; Advaita = Shankara; anekantavada = Jainism; first Jnanpith = Sankara Kurup (1965).
Heritage, UNESCO Sites and Cultural Policy
Current affairs meets static GK
Each year India adds sites; UPSC asks about them. Know the categories, the lists and the institutions.
UNESCO lists

World Heritage Convention (1972; India ratified 1977): cultural, natural and mixed sites. India has 44 World Heritage Sites as of July 2025 (36 cultural, 7 natural, 1 mixed). The Intangible Cultural Heritage convention (2003; India ratified 2005) gives a representative list. India’s ICH elements include Kutiyattam, Vedic chanting, Ramlila, Ramman, Chhau, Kalbelia, Mudiyettu, Sankirtana of Manipur, Yoga (2016), Kumbh Mela (2017), Durga Puja in Kolkata (2021) and Garba (2023).
Recent inscriptions

2021: Dholavira, Ramappa temple (Telangana). 2023: Santiniketan (West Bengal) and Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas. 2024: Moidams (Charaideo, Assam; Ahom burial mounds), India’s 43rd. 2025: Maratha Military Landscapes (12 forts, July 2025), India’s 44th. Tentative list contains many more; India also hosted the 46th World Heritage Committee in New Delhi (July 2024).
Memory of the World and other lists

The Memory of the World Register lists documentary heritage. India’s entries include the Rig Veda manuscripts (2007) and, in 2025, manuscripts of the Bhagavad Gita and the Natyashastra. Check the latest list before the exam. UNESCO Creative Cities Network : Jaipur (crafts), Varanasi (music), Chennai (music), Srinagar (crafts), Kozhikode (literature, 2023) and Gwalior (music, 2023).
Institutions

ASI (1861, Alexander Cunningham): protects monuments under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 ; prohibited area 100 m, regulated area 200 m (2010 amendment). Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972 . INTACH (1984), National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities , Adopt a Heritage (2017, “Apni Dharohar, Apni Pehchaan”). Ministry of Culture: Sangeet Natak Akademi, Sahitya Akademi, Lalit Kala Akademi (all 1950s), National Museum, ICCR.
Constitution and policy

Article 29 (right to conserve culture), Article 49 (DPSP: protect monuments), Article 51A(f) (duty to value the composite culture), and Entry 67 of Union List (ancient monuments of national importance), Entry 12 of State List. The Heritage cities scheme HRIDAY (2015) and PRASAD (pilgrimage), Swadesh Darshan and the Central Vista are policy tools. Heritage by law includes folk and intangible forms through the Guru-Shishya scheme.
Conservation versus development

Tourism pressures at Taj Mahal, Hampi and Khajuraho; encroachments; commercial use of monuments for events; restoration versus preservation (Ayodhya and Konark restoration choices). The Supreme Court’s Taj Trapezium orders and Vishnu Bhagwan’s case show tension. Some argue for community-led conservation and local jobs.
Why it matters today

Repatriation of antiquities (hundreds of objects returned in the last decade), the Bodhgaya and Ajanta tourism circuits and the push for new inscriptions show heritage as soft power. Debates about renaming and the Places of Worship Act 1991 show the legal side.
The six criteria for a World Heritage Site

A site is not listed just because it is old or beautiful. UNESCO applies criteria. A cultural site must meet at least one of six criteria, labelled (i) to (vi). They cover a masterpiece of human creative genius, an exchange of influences, a testimony to a tradition, an outstanding example of a building or landscape type, a link with ideas or beliefs, and other tests set by the Committee. A natural site must meet one of four criteria, (vii) to (x), such as superlative natural beauty or ongoing ecological processes. A mixed site meets both sets. Each site must also show authenticity and integrity, meaning it is genuinely what it claims to be and is not badly damaged. Why this matters for India Many Indian sites are listed for their craft or their role in a wider exchange of ideas. For example, Hampi and the Ajanta caves are cultural sites. The listing is a promise to protect the site, and it can bring tourism and money, but also the risk of over-development. Exam trap: a site is not listed because a government wants it. Listing is decided by the World Heritage Committee on the basis of the nomination dossier and expert reports. How it is asked: Prelims asks which kind of site is natural or mixed, or what authenticity means. Mains asks how World Heritage status helps conservation, and what pressures a listed site can face.
How to answer

“What steps has India taken to protect its cultural heritage?” “Mention World Heritage Sites inscribed recently and the criteria.” Prelims tip: Know the latest inscriptions and the difference between WHS (tangible) and ICH (intangible). Always check the current number from UNESCO or the Ministry of Culture.
European Companies and the Battle of Plassey
A trading company became a state

Trade, not conquest, brought Europeans to India. Within about 150 years of Vasco da Gama landing at Calicut (1498), one company held the richest province of India. Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764) are the hinge of modern Indian history. UPSC asks two things again and again: why the English won over other Europeans, and how a trading firm became a ruler.
The order of arrival

Portuguese : Vasco da Gama, 1498. Albuquerque took Goa in 1510. Their cartaz (naval pass) system controlled sea trade. Dutch : United East India Company, 1602. Centred on the spice islands of Indonesia, with posts such as Pulicat. English : East India Company chartered 31 December 1600. First factory at Surat, 1613. Danes : 1616; Serampore and Tranquebar. French : Compagnie des Indes, 1664 under Colbert. Pondicherry, founded 1674.
Why the English won

Historians offer several reasons. Sea power : the Royal Navy was stronger than the French fleet. Finance : a stable parliamentary government, a strong bank system and company shareholders who wanted dividends. Base : Bengal, Bombay and Madras were rich and could fund wars, while Pondicherry could not. Leaders : Clive and Eyre Coote against a faction-ridden French command. Industrial change and a trained army also helped later. The French were also distracted by wars in Europe and had less state backing than expected.
The Carnatic Wars

Three wars were fought on the Coromandel coast between the English and French (1746 to 1763), tied to the Austrian Succession and Seven Years’ wars in Europe. The first showed that a small, disciplined European-drilled force could beat large Indian armies (the battle of St Thome, 1746). Dupleix backed rival claimants in Hyderabad and the Carnatic. Clive’s seizure of Arcot (1751) turned the tide. The third war ended with the French defeat at Wandiwash (1760, Eyre Coote). The Treaty of Paris (1763) left Pondicherry to the French as a trading post only.
Plassey, 23 June 1757

Siraj-ud-daulah became Nawab of Bengal in 1756. He seized Calcutta (the “Black Hole” story is doubted by many historians). Clive retook it and then plotted with the nawab’s own commanders. At Plassey, Mir Jafar , the commander, held back his troops. Others in the plot included Rai Durlabh, Yar Lutuf Khan, the banker Jagat Seth and Omichand. The battle was little more than a skirmish, yet it gave the Company the throne of Bengal in all but name. Mir Jafar became nawab and paid huge sums.
Buxar and the Diwani

Mir Qasim, Mir Jafar’s son-in-law, tried to rule independently and abolished internal duties. He joined Shuja-ud-daula of Awadh and Shah Alam II, the Mughal emperor. They were beaten at Buxar, 1764 (Hector Munro). By the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) Clive got the Diwani (revenue rights) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa from Shah Alam II. The Nawab kept the nizamat (policing and justice). This was the dual government (1765 to 1772), power without responsibility, which Warren Hastings ended.
Was Plassey a battle or a conspiracy?

Nationalist historians such as Bipan Chandra stress that Plassey was won by treachery and by Bengal’s own elite, not by arms. Buxar was the real military test. Yet Plassey mattered because it handed the Company Bengal’s wealth. This funded armies and bought Indian-made goods with Indian revenue, a point Dadabhai Naoroji later used in his drain theory. Some historians, such as C. A. Bayly, say the Company’s rise also depended on Indian bankers and local elites who chose to back it.
Why it matters today

Bengal’s early colonisation shaped Calcutta’s rise as capital (till 1911) and the Permanent Settlement later. The memory of dependence on foreign trading power is behind India’s caution about economic dependence and strategic autonomy. Goa remained Portuguese until 1961, and Pondicherry stayed French until its de facto transfer in 1954. These are the last pieces of European empire in India.
Plassey: a battle and a turning point

Plassey on 23 June 1757 is often called the start of British rule in India, but it was a battle followed by a long process. Robert Clive commanded the Company's forces. Siraj-ud-daulah, the Nawab of Bengal, led a much larger army, but some of his commanders did not fight with full commitment. Mir Jafar, a senior commander, made a secret deal with Clive. After the battle the Company made him Nawab. The Company gained money, trade rights and a growing hold over Bengal's revenue. Commonly quoted figures put the Company side at about 3,000 men and the Nawab's side at about 50,000. Treat these as approximate. From Plassey to the Diwani Mir Qasim tried to resist the Company's trade abuses and was defeated at Buxar in 1764.
